title: Black Tupelo: Ancient Black Tupelo Trees You Can Visit
meta_description: An eastern wetland tree, planted in cities for its red autumn leaves. Central Park's was put in the ground in 1858, four years before the Reservoir.
intro: Black tupelo is a tree of eastern North American swamps that cities plant for its glossy leaves, which turn deep red in autumn. The oldest of ours is in the Ramble in Central Park, where documentation places its planting at 1858, during the park's original construction and four years before the Reservoir was dug. In Atlanta, a champion in a Poncey-Highland yard has been on the city's list since 2006, at 2.8 metres round and 27.4 metres tall, and it is viewed from the sidewalk. And in Madison, the University of Wisconsin Arboretum bought a seedling in 1956, grew it on in the nursery, and on 3 October 1961 planted it by what is now the Visitor Center. In the wild the species grows in only one Wisconsin county, yet this one became the state's champion at 11.9 metres.
